lesson.title: Vapor Pressure: The Molecular Tug of War at a Liquid's Surface
lesson.summary: Vapor pressure is the pressure exerted by a liquid's vapor once evaporation and condensation reach dynamic equilibrium, and it is the quantity that determines exactly when and why a liquid boils.
lesson.body:
Inside a sealed container holding some liquid and empty space above it, molecules are not sitting still. Kinetic molecular theory describes those liquid molecules as having a spread of kinetic energies, not one uniform speed, and at any instant some of the fastest moving molecules near the surface have enough energy to break free of their neighbors' intermolecular attractions and escape into the space above as vapor. At the same time, vapor molecules are colliding with the surface and being recaptured back into the liquid. Once the rate of escape equals the rate of recapture, the amount of vapor stops changing, and the pressure that vapor exerts on the container is the vapor pressure of the liquid at that temperature.

This dynamic equilibrium is the same idea that underlies boiling and condensation. Vapor pressure rises sharply as temperature increases, because a warmer liquid has more molecules in that high energy tail able to escape at any given moment. Boiling is what happens when a liquid's vapor pressure climbs high enough to equal the external pressure pressing down on it: at that point, vapor can form as bubbles anywhere inside the liquid, not only evaporate slowly from the surface. That is why the normal boiling point, the one printed on data tables, is specifically defined as the temperature at which a substance's vapor pressure equals exactly 1 atm (101.325 kPa, or 760 mmHg).

Water's vapor pressure at 25°C is about 23.8 mmHg, far below 760 mmHg, which is exactly why a glass of water at room temperature does not boil, it just evaporates slowly as some molecules escape from the surface. By the time the temperature reaches 100°C, water's vapor pressure has climbed all the way to 760 mmHg, matching sea level atmospheric pressure, and boiling begins.

Altitude changes the target the vapor pressure has to hit. Denver's atmospheric pressure, at roughly 0.83 atm, converts to about 0.83 multiplied by 101.325 kPa, or about 84.1 kPa, noticeably lower than sea level's 101.3 kPa. Since boiling only requires the liquid's vapor pressure to match whatever the local atmospheric pressure happens to be, water in Denver reaches its boiling point at a lower vapor pressure target and therefore at a lower temperature, around 95°C instead of 100°C. That is a real, practical consequence of the same equilibrium described above, not a separate phenomenon.

Vapor pressure is also a direct readout of how strongly a liquid's molecules attract each other. Liquids held together by weak intermolecular forces evaporate readily and have high vapor pressure at a given temperature; chemists call these volatile. Liquids with strong hydrogen bonding or ionic character resist escaping and have low vapor pressure; they are far less volatile. That same competition between escaping and staying, between weak and strong intermolecular attraction, is exactly the idea that reappears when comparing how easily different substances dissolve into one another.
